name: APIs and Service Boundaries Interview Prep
description: 20 advanced questions on API design, service decomposition, versioning, backward compatibility, idempotency, and cross-service boundaries.

cards.front: 1. What makes an API easy to evolve?
cards.back: An evolvable API has clear contracts, additive changes, stable identifiers, and explicit deprecation policy. Compatibility is a design requirement, not a post-launch cleanup task.

cards.front: 2. When should you split a service boundary?
cards.back: Split when ownership, scaling, deployment cadence, or failure domain meaningfully differ. If two parts of the system must always change together, splitting them may create more pain than value.

cards.front: 3. Why is backward compatibility so important?
cards.back: Because clients, jobs, and downstream services will not all upgrade at once. Backward compatibility lets you ship without forcing coordinated downtime across the ecosystem.

cards.front: 4. What is the difference between REST and gRPC in design interviews?
cards.back: REST is simpler and broadly accessible, while gRPC is often better for internal service-to-service calls with stricter contracts and lower overhead. The right choice depends on interoperability, latency, and tooling.

cards.front: 5. How should you model idempotent writes?
cards.back: Use client-generated request IDs, deduplication, or natural idempotency keys so retries do not create duplicates. This is especially important when the network can drop responses after the server already committed.

cards.front: 6. Why are pagination and filtering part of API design?
cards.back: Because unbounded reads are a reliability and performance problem, not just a UI detail. Pagination strategy also affects sort stability, consistency, and future compatibility.

cards.front: 7. How do you think about ownership across service boundaries?
cards.back: Each service should own its data and business rules, even if other services depend on them. Clear ownership reduces ambiguity, duplicate logic, and accidental coupling.

cards.front: 8. What is an anti-corruption layer and when do you need one?
cards.back: An ACL translates between external models and your internal domain so a legacy or third-party contract does not infect your core design. It is useful when external semantics are messy or unstable.

cards.front: 9. Why are versioned schemas often better than versioned endpoints?
cards.back: Schema versioning can preserve a single endpoint while still evolving payload shape and contract semantics. That keeps the API surface smaller and usually simplifies client adoption.

cards.front: 10. How do you design for partial failure across services?
cards.back: Use timeouts, retries, fallbacks, and bounded isolation so one bad dependency does not freeze the entire request path. Service boundaries only help if the failure domains are truly independent.

cards.front: 11. What makes an API hard to debug?
cards.back: Hidden side effects, unclear ownership, inconsistent error shapes, and vague request correlation all make debugging painful. Great APIs are boring to operate because they are predictable.

cards.front: 12. How should errors be modeled in APIs?
cards.back: Errors should be stable, machine-readable, and distinct enough for callers to know whether to retry, fix input, or escalate. Vague generic errors push complexity into every client.

cards.front: 13. Why does API idempotency matter for mobile and flaky networks?
cards.back: Mobile clients and flaky links create duplicate submissions and ambiguous outcomes. Idempotency turns uncertainty into safe retry behavior.

cards.front: 14. What is the danger of too many service boundaries?
cards.back: Excessive boundaries create chatty dependencies, operational overhead, and slower product delivery. A good decomposition should reduce coupling, not just multiply services.

cards.front: 15. How do you think about read models versus write models?
cards.back: Write models protect invariants and business rules; read models optimize retrieval and user experience. Separating them can simplify the system when read and write needs diverge.

cards.front: 16. What should be documented in an API contract?
cards.back: Input and output shapes, error semantics, auth requirements, rate limits, idempotency, and compatibility expectations. A contract should prevent guesswork for consumers.

cards.front: 17. How do you introduce a breaking API change safely?
cards.back: Use parallel fields or endpoints, migrate clients incrementally, observe adoption, and only then retire the old shape. Breaking changes are a rollout problem as much as a code problem.

cards.front: 18. What is the role of service ownership in incident response?
cards.back: Ownership determines who gets paged, who can mitigate, and who can safely make trade-offs under pressure. If ownership is unclear, recovery gets slower.

cards.front: 19. Why do APIs need rate limiting?
cards.back: Rate limiting protects the backend from abusive, accidental, or bursty traffic and helps enforce fairness across clients. It is both a capacity tool and an abuse-prevention tool.

cards.front: 20. When is a monolith a better choice than service splitting?
cards.back: When the domain is small, the team is small, and the boundaries are still unstable, a monolith can be simpler and safer. Staff engineers should split only when the split clearly improves ownership or scale.

author: Gemini
